topic: Claude Code Effort Levels A/B Test: What Reduced Effort Means for Coding Agents

key_points: Effort is NOT just 'thinking time' — it controls how much work Claude does overall: how many files it reads, how much it verifies, and how far it pushes through a multi-step task before checking in.
At higher effort, Claude reads files, runs tests, and double-checks before coming back; at lower effort it would rather ask for more context than spend tokens figuring things out on its own.
Model selection = capability (fixed weights, knowledge). Effort = thoroughness/behavior. These are two orthogonal dials.
If Claude has full context, clearly tried, and still got it wrong -> pick a more capable model. If it skipped a file, didn't run tests, or bailed mid-refactor -> pick a higher effort level.
Start with default effort levels per model and tune as a general preference, not task-by-task.
'Raise effort when the model was lazy; switch models when it was ignorant.' Thoroughness gap = /effort problem; knowledge/capability gap = model problem.
Effort affects ALL tokens in the response (text, explanations, tool calls, function args, and thinking when active) — it does not require thinking to be enabled.
Effort is 'a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget' — max doesn't buy a guaranteed number of reasoning tokens, it buys a Claude that acts like it has all the time in the world.
Five levels: max / xhigh / high(default) / medium / low — with a table of thinking behavior and when to reach for each.
Availability differs by model: Opus 4.6/Sonnet 4.6 lack xhigh; unsupported levels silently fall back to the highest supported one at or below.
Effort scale is calibrated PER MODEL — same level name is not the same underlying value across models; run a fresh effort sweep on Opus 5 rather than reusing old settings.
Most people default too high and pay for it — provides a task-to-level routing table (lint fix=low, scoped feature=high default, stubborn debug=xhigh, architecture=max).
Claude Opus 4.8 added five effort levels (low through max).
Explains when to use each level and how effort affects token spend — matching effort to task complexity is the key cost lever.
High effort increases token consumption and cost; low effort minimizes spend on routine work.

A/B test context: Anthropic sometimes tests API serving configs in Claude Code before rollout; one running test mapped the numerical effort value differently (users reported effort showing '10' on high).

Official team response (Thariq, Claude Code team): the scale isn't 0-100, the number isn't meaningful on its own, and 'the effort you selected is the effort you're getting' — in-depth evals confirmed it doesn't affect model performance.

stats.fact: Effort controls all response tokens — text, explanations, tool calls, function arguments, and thinking when active — and does not require thinking to be enabled.

The A/B test that surfaced in the community (Aug 2026) mapped a numerical effort value differently so Claude reported '10' on high; Anthropic stated the scale isn't 0-100 and the number is not meaningful on its own.
stats.source: Hacker News thread 49401549 + Thariq (Claude Code team) official response

stats.fact: Anthropic confirmed via in-depth evals that the A/B test does not affect model performance.
stats.source: Thariq, Claude Code team, Hacker News 49401549

stats.fact: Unsupported effort levels silently fall back to the highest supported level at or below the one set (e.g. xhigh runs as high on Opus 4.6).
The effort scale is calibrated per model — the same level name (e.g. 'medium') represents a different underlying value across different models.
Anthropic recommends running a fresh effort sweep on Opus 5 rather than reusing effort settings carried over from an earlier model.

At lower effort, Claude combines operations into fewer tool calls, skips preamble, and uses terse confirmations; at higher effort it makes more tool calls, explains plans first, and writes longer summaries/comments.

angles: Interpret the A/B test as a teachable moment: effort numbers are a behavioral signal, not a literal 0-100 dial — users should stop treating reported values as ground truth.
Decision framework: 'raise effort when lazy, switch model when ignorant' — give readers a reusable heuristic instead of a config dump.
Cost angle: most users default too high and waste tokens; matching effort to task complexity is the biggest token/cost lever in Claude Code.
Per-model calibration gotcha: your 'medium' on one model is not your 'medium' on another — why re-running an effort sweep matters when upgrading models.
Practical routing table translating common tasks (lint fix, feature, debug, refactor, architecture) to a starting effort level.
How to verify your effort setting and detect regressions (/feedback, effort statusline plugins, asking Claude what level it is — with the caveat that the number isn't meaningful on its own).
